title: Chapter 5 – FIDE Swiss Rules: Mock Exam

questions.text: Which pairing system is the standard FIDE Swiss pairing system?

options.text: The Baku Acceleration System
The Dutch System
The Scheveningen System
The Berger System

questions.explanation: As per Article C04.3, the Dutch System is the standard FIDE Swiss pairing system. Players are divided into score brackets and the top half is paired against the bottom half within each bracket.

questions.text: In a Swiss system, can a player be paired against the same opponent twice?

options.text: Yes, if they are the only players with the same score
Yes, but only in the final round
No, a player is never paired against the same opponent twice
Only if both players request it

questions.explanation: As per Article C04.1, a player is never paired against the same opponent twice in a Swiss system. This is a fundamental absolute rule of all Swiss pairing systems.

questions.text: In the Baku Acceleration system, what are virtual points used for?

options.text: To award bonus prizes to top-rated players
To create more competitive pairings by making top players meet earlier
To compensate players who receive a bye
To calculate the final standings when scores are tied

questions.explanation: As per Article C04.5.1, in the Baku Acceleration system, top-ranked players receive virtual points in early rounds to create more competitive pairings. This ensures top players meet earlier, reducing easy wins in the first rounds.

questions.text: When must pairings be published in a Swiss tournament?

options.text: After the round has started
Before the start of each round
Only in the last round
Only if a player requests to see them

questions.explanation: As per Article C04.2D, pairings must be published before the start of each round. Players have the right to check their pairing and colour. Errors discovered before the game starts must be corrected.

questions.text: How are late entries treated in a Swiss tournament?

options.text: They are not allowed to enter after the first round
They receive full points for all missed rounds automatically
They receive zero score or a half-point bye for each missed round as specified
They are always paired in the last group regardless of rating

questions.explanation: As per Article C04.2C, late entries receive a score of zero for each missed round or a half-point bye as specified in the tournament regulations. The arbiter decides and must announce the policy in advance.

questions.text: What is the colour allocation rule in the Dutch System when two players in the same score group are paired?

options.text: The higher-rated player always gets White
Colours alternate based on each player's colour history, with the player due White getting it
The player with fewer wins gets White
Colour is decided by coin toss each round

questions.explanation: Per Article C04.3, the Dutch System allocates colours based on the colour history of each player. Each player should ideally alternate colours, and the player who is 'due White' (based on previous colours) gets White.

questions.text: What is a 'bye' in a Swiss tournament?

options.text: A draw agreed before the game starts
A round where a player has no opponent and receives a score without playing
A player's right to withdraw from one round without penalty
An extra round added at the end of the tournament

questions.explanation: Per Article C04.2B, a bye is given to a player who has no opponent in a round (usually due to an odd number of players). The player with the bye typically receives half a point or, for a requested bye, as specified by the regulations.

questions.text: In the Dutch System, how are players divided for pairing within each score group?

options.text: Randomly shuffled within each group
Top half (S1) paired against bottom half (S2) by rating order
First player plays last player, second plays second-last, etc.
Players are paired based on their colour history only

questions.explanation: Per Article C04.3, within each score bracket players are sorted by rating. The bracket is split into S1 (top half) and S2 (bottom half). The top player of S1 is paired with the top player of S2, and so on.

questions.text: How many rounds are typically recommended for a Swiss tournament with 64 players?

options.text: 5 rounds
6 rounds
7 rounds
9 rounds

questions.explanation: Per Article C04.1, the recommended number of rounds for a Swiss tournament is approximately log₂(N) where N is the number of players. For 64 players: log₂(64) = 6 rounds. This ensures a clear winner can emerge.

questions.text: When may the arbiter deviate from the standard Swiss pairing rules?

options.text: Whenever the arbiter personally prefers a different pairing
Only to avoid byes or to prevent violation of absolute criteria like same-opponent-twice
At any time, as the arbiter has full discretion
Only in the last round, to ensure a decisive final game

questions.explanation: Per Article C04.2, the arbiter can only deviate from standard Swiss pairing rules when strictly necessary — for example, to avoid giving a bye to a player who has already had one, or to prevent the same two players meeting again.
